title: Typed Reactivity and Composition API
learning_outcomes: Explain the optional specialist topic “Typed Reactivity and Composition API” in a JavaScript-first Vue project.
Identify the contract or code-organization problem the technique is intended to solve.
State the tooling/runtime assumptions and one limitation.

content.intro: This lesson studies Typed Reactivity and Composition API within TypeScript and Large-Scale Code Organization. The source PDF subtopics are preserved below and connected to an original working-style example.
content.why_it_matters: Types can make component contracts more explicit, but they add tooling and should fit the needs of the project and team.

content_blocks.title: Typed Reactivity and Composition API: Static types and runtime validation
content_blocks.alt_text: Static types and runtime validation diagram for lesson 111: Typed Reactivity and Composition API. Treat network payloads as runtime values → Use tooling to catch inconsistent assumptions → Validate untrusted data before relying on it
content_blocks.caption: Type-safety flow: compile-time contracts support development but do not replace validation of runtime data.

content_blocks.title: The idea in context
content_blocks.text: TypeScript is an optional specialization for larger Vue codebases; the core teaching path and repository files remain JavaScript/JSX. This lesson focuses on Typed Reactivity and Composition API. Start by naming the state, component, browser behavior, or deployment boundary involved; then predict what should change and test the smallest example.

items.title: Typing refs and reactive objects
items.text: For Typing refs and reactive objects, identify the reactive source that changes and the value or side effect that depends on it. Prefer computed values for derived data; use watchers when a change must trigger work outside pure derivation, and keep dependencies explicit.

items.title: Typing computed values
items.text: For Typing computed values, identify the reactive source that changes and the value or side effect that depends on it. Prefer computed values for derived data; use watchers when a change must trigger work outside pure derivation, and keep dependencies explicit.

items.title: Typing watchers
items.text: For Typing watchers, identify the reactive source that changes and the value or side effect that depends on it. Prefer computed values for derived data; use watchers when a change must trigger work outside pure derivation, and keep dependencies explicit.

items.title: Typing template refs
items.text: For Typing template refs, identify the reactive source that changes and the value or side effect that depends on it. Prefer computed values for derived data; use watchers when a change must trigger work outside pure derivation, and keep dependencies explicit.

content_blocks.code:
<script setup lang="ts">
import { ref } from 'vue'
const count = ref<number>(0)
const props = defineProps<{ label: string }>()
</script>
<template><button>{{ props.label }}: {{ count }}</button></template>
content_blocks.expected_output: The type annotations help the tooling check component contracts; the runtime still receives JavaScript values. This is an optional example, not a new file in this CodeLeaf patch.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Use only in a separate TypeScript-enabled Vue project that has compatible Vue language tooling. The CodeLeaf source patch itself adds no .ts/.tsx files.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the initial values or original code, reload the development app/test, and repeat once with a boundary or failure case. Remove temporary logs and test data before committing.

content_blocks.title: Guided example
content_blocks.text: Work through Typed Reactivity and Composition API with a predict–change–verify loop. First state the expected UI or console output. Change only the relevant input/state value, then observe the result. Compare it with the expected output in the code block; if it differs, check the exact file, runtime/version, browser Console, and network response before widening the investigation.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Extend the example to include “Typing computed values”. Keep the same behavior for the ordinary input, then try an empty, invalid, repeated, or failure condition that makes sense for the example. Record the expected result before testing.

items.title: Assuming behavior instead of checking it
items.text: Write down the expected result and reproduce the issue in the smallest possible example; inspect the browser Console and the exact reactive value or request.

items.title: Ignoring an edge case
items.text: Try empty input, a missing item, repeated interaction, a failed request, or unmounting while work is pending; handle the case explicitly.

items.title: Putting every responsibility in one component
items.text: Separate display, reusable logic, API service, and shared state when that boundary makes the behavior easier to test and explain.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: Remember: TypeScript is an optional specialization for larger Vue codebases; the core teaching path and repository files remain JavaScript/JSX. For Typed Reactivity and Composition API, keep the example small, verify the rendered or logged result, and consult the official references when behavior depends on a specific Vue or ecosystem version.

content_blocks.title: Accessibility, version, and runtime notes
content_blocks.text: TypeScript is an optional specialization from the supplied PDF. The CodeLeaf repository patch remains JavaScript/JSX-only and adds no .ts/.tsx files. A TypeScript snippet is illustrative and requires a separate Vue project with language tooling. Runtime validation is still needed for API data.

content.task: Create a small example for “Typed Reactivity and Composition API” that applies “Typing refs and reactive objects”, predicts the expected result, and verifies a relevant boundary case.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example demonstrates the named Vue concept rather than only mentioning it.
The expected output or observable behavior is written down and can be checked locally.
At least one boundary, loading, invalid-input, or failure case is tested or explicitly reasoned about.
The example uses semantic/accessible interaction patterns and does not treat frontend state as authoritative security.
hints: Start with the smallest observable part of “Typing refs and reactive objects”.
Predict the output before changing one input at a time.
Use the browser Console, Vue DevTools, or the appropriate test runner to isolate a mismatch.

common_mistakes.problem: The example only covers the happy path.
common_mistakes.why: Real interfaces receive empty values, delayed responses, invalid input, and failed requests.
common_mistakes.fix: Add one realistic edge/failure case and state its expected behavior.

common_mistakes.problem: The code assumes an API or feature exists in every runtime.
common_mistakes.why: Tool and API support depends on Vue, the build tool, or the chosen SSR/test framework.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the linked official reference and record the runtime/version assumption.

summary: Typed Reactivity and Composition API belongs to the broader area TypeScript and Large-Scale Code Organization.
The main concept to practice is Typing refs and reactive objects.
Verify a normal result and one meaningful boundary case before using the pattern in a production feature.
